steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on proof theory for extensions of K5 and uniform Lyndon interpolation. Give background on uniform interpolation and its Lyndon variant, explain our long-term proof-theoretic program, and introduce the layered sequent calculi, the termination and complexity result, and the interpolation proof for K5.

3. Long-term goal: proof-theoretic UIP via multisequent calculi
- goal: general proof-theoretic method to (re)prove UIP for modal logics via multisequent calculi (nested sequents, hypersequents, labelled hypersequents, etc.)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The uniform interpolation property (UIP) is an important property of a logic. It is a strengthening of the Craig interpolation property (CIP), because the interpolants only depend on one formula of an implication, either the premise or the conclusion. A lot of work has been done on proving the UIP, and it has turned out to be useful in various areas of computer science, including knowledge representation and description logics. Early results on the UIP in modal logic include positive results for logics \mathsf{GL} and \mathsf{K}, proved semantically (and independently by several authors), and negative results for logics {\sf S4} and {\sf K4}. A proof-theoretic method for proving the UIP was first proposed for intuitionistic propositional logic, and later it was adapted to modal logics such as \mathsf{K} and \mathsf{T}. In a series of papers a general proof-theoretic method was developed for proving the UIP for many classical and intuitionistic (non-)normal modal logics and substructural (modal) logics, based on the form of the rules of their sequent calculi.

Besides the UIP, we are also interested in the uniform Lyndon interpolation property (ULIP). The ULIP strengthens the UIP in the sense that the interpolants have to respect the polarities of the propositional variables involved. Kurahashi was the first to introduce this property, and he proved it for several normal modal logics with a semantic method that uses layered bisimulations. A sequent-based proof-theoretic method has been used to show the ULIP for several non-normal modal logics and conditional logics.

Our long-term goal is a general proof-theoretic method to (re)prove the UIP for modal logics via multisequent calculi (i.e., nested sequents, hypersequents, labelled hypersequents, etc.). The proof-theoretic treatment is constructive, unlike many other ways of proving interpolation, because it also gives an algorithm for constructing uniform interpolants. For this goal we build on the modular treatment of multicomponent calculi that was used to prove the CIP for modal and intermediate logics. Some first steps have been made: the UIP was reproved for modal logics {\sf K}, {\sf D}, and {\sf T} via nested sequents and for {\sf S5} via hypersequents, and this was the first time it was proved proof-theoretically for {\sf S5}.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The uniform interpolation property (UIP) is an important property of a logic. It is a strengthening of the Craig interpolation property (CIP), because the interpolants only depend on one formula of an implication, either the premise or the conclusion. A lot of work has been done on proving the UIP, and it has turned out to be useful in various areas of computer science, including knowledge representation and description logics. Early results on the UIP in modal logic include positive results for logics \mathsf{GL} and \mathsf{K}, proved semantically (and independently by several authors), and negative results for logics {\sf S4} and {\sf K4}. A proof-theoretic method for proving the UIP was first proposed for intuitionistic propositional logic, and later it was adapted to modal logics such as \mathsf{K} and \mathsf{T}. In a series of papers a general proof-theoretic method was developed for proving the UIP for many classical and intuitionistic (non-)normal modal logics and substructural (modal) logics, based on the form of the rules of their sequent calculi.

Besides the UIP, we are also interested in the uniform Lyndon interpolation property (ULIP). The ULIP strengthens the UIP in the sense that the interpolants have to respect the polarities of the propositional variables involved. Kurahashi was the first to introduce this property, and he proved it for several normal modal logics with a semantic method that uses layered bisimulations. A sequent-based proof-theoretic method has been used to show the ULIP for several non-normal modal logics and conditional logics.

Our long-term goal is a general proof-theoretic method to (re)prove the UIP for modal logics via multisequent calculi (i.e., nested sequents, hypersequents, labelled hypersequents, etc.). The proof-theoretic treatment is constructive, unlike many other ways of proving interpolation, because it also gives an algorithm for constructing uniform interpolants. For this goal we build on the modular treatment of multicomponent calculi that was used to prove the CIP for modal and intermediate logics. Some first steps have been made: the UIP was reproved for modal logics {\sf K}, {\sf D}, and {\sf T} via nested sequents and for {\sf S5} via hypersequents, and this was the first time it was proved proof-theoretically for {\sf S5}.

In this paper we focus on the logics {\sf K5}, {\sf KD5}, {\sf K45}, {\sf KD45}, {\sf KB5}, and {\sf S5}. Kurahashi derived the ULIP for these logics from their local tabularity and their Lyndon interpolation property (LIP).

To get a modular proof-theoretic treatment, we introduce a new form of multisequent calculi for these logics, which we call layered sequent calculi. Their structure is inspired by the structure of the Kripke frames for these logics. For {\sf S5} this gives standard hypersequents. For {\sf K5} and {\sf KD5} the calculi we present are similar to grafted hypersequent calculi, but without explicit weakening. There are also other proof systems that are less related, including analytic cut-free sequent systems for {\sf K5} and {\sf KD5}, cut-free sequent calculi for {\sf K45} and {\sf KD45}, and nested sequent calculi for modal logics.

The layered sequent calculi in this paper use a strong version of termination that only relies on a local loop-check based on saturation. For all of the logics we consider, this gives a decision procedure that runs in co-NP time, and this is therefore optimal. We give a semantic completeness proof by constructing a countermodel from a failed proof search.

Finally, we use layered sequents to give the first proof-theoretic proof of the ULIP for {\sf K5}. We adapted the method from the work where the UIP is proved for {\sf S5} based on hypersequents. We give an algorithm that constructs uniform Lyndon interpolants purely by syntactic means, using the termination strategy of the proof search. To show that the constructed interpolants are correct, we use model-theoretic techniques that are inspired by bisimulation quantification in the setting of uniform Lyndon interpolation.

For this goal we build on the modular treatment of multicomponent calculi that was used to prove the CIP for modal and intermediate logics [14,15,16,17,18]. For {\sf S5}, this results in standard hypersequents [25,26,27]. For {\sf K5} and {\sf KD5}, the calculi we present are similar to the grafted hypersequent calculi in [28], but without explicit weakening. Other, less related, proof systems include analytic cut-free sequent systems for {\sf K5} and {\sf KD5} [29], cut-free sequent calculi for {\sf K45} and {\sf KD45} [30], and nested sequent calculi for modal logics [31].

The layered sequent calculi introduced in this paper adopt a strong version of termination that relies only on a local loop-check based on saturation. For all the concerned logics, this yields a decision procedure running in co-NP time, which is therefore optimal [32]. We provide a semantic completeness proof via a countermodel construction from failed proof search.

Finally, we use layered sequents to provide the first proof-theoretic proof of the ULIP for {\sf K5}. The method is adapted from [21,20], where the UIP is proved for {\sf S5} based on hypersequents. We provide an algorithm that constructs uniform Lyndon interpolants purely by syntactic means, using the termination strategy of the proof search. To show the correctness of the constructed interpolants, we use model-theoretic techniques inspired by bisimulation quantification in the setting of uniform Lyndon interpolation [12].
